::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Can you explain the absolute value sign when integrating $\int_{-1}^{1}dx \int_{0}^{x^2} \sqrt{x^2-y} dy$?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2713373/can-you-explain-the-absolute-value-sign-when-integrating-int-11dx-int), asked by [Juan](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/269726/juan) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2018-03-29; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> I'm doing homework on the following integral:
> $$\int_{-1}^{1}dx \int_{0}^{x^2} \sqrt{x^2-y} dy$$
> And here is the answer:
> [![Why the absolute value][q-1]][q-1]
>
>
>   [q-1]: bP7Lh.png
>
> I try to think about it, but I couldn't answer why there is an absolute value sign in the third expression at $x^3$. Can somebody explain it for me why? Thank you! :D
:::

To elaborate on the existing answers, notice what happens when you forget that $\sqrt{u^2} = |u|$ and substitute $u$ instead:
$$I_2 = \dots = \int_{-1}^1 \int_0^{x^2} \sqrt{x^2-y}\,dy\,dx
  =  \color{red}{\frac{2}{3}\int_{-1}^1 x^3\,dx} = 0$$
At this point, you should notice there must be some mistake. 
The integrand is nonnegative so the integral should be positive.
